The person-evidence agent found **four gaps** in the `pe_` links for the 1860 census record (`ark:/61903/1:1:MABC`):

| Assertion | Fact type | Linked? |
|-----------|-----------|---------|

| a_009 | birth (age 15, ~1845, Ireland) | ❌ No link at all |

The 1850 census handled this correctly with `pe_006`, making this gap especially clear.

I1 (Patrick Flynn) was already in the tree before the 1860 census was linked, so a `same_person` score should have been computed and recorded. Without it, the `confident` rating on pe_004 cannot be independently audited.

---

### Summary

| Gap | Type |
|-----|------|
| a_008 → I1 missing | Unlinked assertion |
| a_009 → I1 missing | Unlinked assertion |
| a_010 → I2 missing | Missing other-side link (Thomas Flynn) |
| pe_004 match_score null | Confidence rating unverifiable |

If you'd like the agent to create the three missing `pe_` entries and obtain the missing `same_person` score, just say the word.

I now have everything needed for the audit. This is review-only mode — I will produce a written analysis and make no writes.

---

**1860 Census Record Audit**
Record: `ark:/61903/1:1:MABC` — three extracted assertions, all on `record_role: child_2` (Patrick Flynn's persona)

**Assertions and their link status**

| Assertion | Fact type | Linked? | pe_ entry |
|-----------|-----------|---------|-----------|
| a_008 | name ("Patrick Flynn") | No | — |
| a_009 | birth (age 15, ~1845, Ireland) | No | — |
| a_010 | relationship (child of Thomas Flynn, head) | Partially | pe_004 → I1 only |

---

**Gap 1 — a_008 and a_009 are completely unlinked**

The name and birth assertions for Patrick Flynn's child_2 persona on the 1860 census have no `pe_` entries at all. The only assertion on this persona that was linked is the relationship assertion (a_010). All three assertions belong to the same persona (child_2), so they should all carry a link to the same person (I1, Patrick Flynn). Linking only the relationship assertion and skipping the name and birth assertions leaves the audit trail incomplete: a reviewer cannot see that the name "Patrick Flynn" and the age-15/Ireland birth fact were part of what confirmed identity. These two assertions should each have a `pe_` entry pointing to I1 at the same confidence level pe_004 carries.

**Gap 2 — a_010 is missing its other-side link to I2 (Thomas Flynn)**

This is the most significant structural gap. Assertion a_010 reads: "Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position and age consistent with son." Its `structured_value.related_person_role` is `head_of_household`. That means a_010 names two parties: Patrick Flynn (child_2, → I1) and Thomas Flynn (head_of_household, → I2). The cardinality rule requires one `pe_` entry per person an assertion bears on. pe_004 covers the I1 side. There is no pe_ entry covering the I2 side. The 1850 census has this done correctly (pe_006 links a_004 → I2 for the equivalent relationship assertion on that record), but the 1860 counterpart is missing. A link from a_010 to I2 at `probable` would mirror the existing pe_006 pattern.

**Gap 3 — pe_004 has a null match_score despite I1 being a pre-existing person**

pe_004 links a_010 → I1 at `confident`. The `match_score` field is null. I1 (Patrick Flynn) was already in the tree before the 1860 census was linked — his sourceRefs include S1 (1850 census) and S3 (death certificate). That means I1 is not a person minted from the child_2 persona, so a `same_person` call should have been made and its score recorded here. The two legitimate reasons for a null score — the candidate was minted from this very persona, or the tool refused because no persona was reachable — do not apply. Without the score, the `confident` rating on pe_004 cannot be independently audited. The 1850 census link (pe_003 for I2 at score 0.82) shows the pattern that was intended here.

---

**Summary of gaps**

| Gap | Type | Assessment |
|-----|------|------------|
| a_008 → I1 missing | Unlinked assertion | Clear gap; straightforward addition |
| a_009 → I1 missing | Unlinked assertion | Clear gap; straightforward addition |
| a_010 → I2 missing | Missing other-side link | Clear gap; mirrors pe_006 pattern on 1850 census |
| pe_004 match_score null | Calibration concern | Score should exist; `confident` tier unauditable without it |

None of these gaps require a confidence change to pe_004 itself, but gap 3 means the `confident` rating is unverified. If you'd like me to create the three missing `pe_` entries (a_008 → I1, a_009 → I1, and a_010 → I2) and obtain the missing `same_person` score for pe_004, say the word and I'll do that as the next request.

---

The 1860 census record has three assertions that are either fully unlinked or only half-linked: the name and birth facts for Patrick Flynn were never connected to him in the tree, and the household relationship that names Thomas Flynn as head was never linked to Thomas Flynn's own person entry. The score that should back up the confident match rating for Patrick is also absent, so that rating is currently unverifiable. Authorizing the linking work would close all four gaps in one pass.

**Conflict found — your confirmation needed before proceeding.**

The baptism records Patrick Flynn's christening on **12 March 1858** at Kilrush. The tree person I1 (Patrick Flynn) carries a birth year of **~1845** — a 13-year gap. Irish Catholic baptisms followed birth within days, so a christening 13 years after the recorded birth is a presumptive contradiction, not ordinary date noise.

This means the links for the child persona (a_001 and a_003) to I1 can only be written at `speculative` confidence — that is: "possibly the same person, but a core date conflicts and the record does not explain the gap (e.g. no note of a conditional or adult baptism)."

**What you need to decide:**

One of the following is true:
1. The ~1845 birth year for I1 in the tree is an estimate that is simply wrong, and Patrick's actual birth year is closer to 1858. In that case a speculative link now — resolved to `confident` once the year is corrected — is appropriate.
2. This is a different Patrick Flynn, and the 1858 Kilrush baptism belongs to someone else.
3. There is an unusual circumstance (delayed baptism, conditional baptism) the record does not state, which could explain the gap.

- Materializing the child persona's christening fact onto I1.

Do you want me to create the two speculative child-to-I1 links? Or does the 1845 birth year need revisiting first?

The move from Cranfield, England to Salt Lake, Utah is properly explained via the LDS emigration corridor documented in the wiki. No fabricated material or unsupported claims. The skill correctly noted Sarah's absence from the 1880 census as an open research question rather than forcing a match.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed all required work: linked all four persons from both the 1860 and 1880 censuses to the correct tree persons (I1–I4), created 20 person-evidence entries covering all assertions, materialized facts into the tree with proper source references, and flagged the Sarah Pratt research gap. Both census households were fully processed with no silent omissions.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. place_search calls for Cranfield and Salt Lake matched expected patterns (~Cranfield, ~Salt Lake). place_distance correctly compared England and Utah locations. wiki_read correctly targeted Utah_Emigration_and_Immigration. same_person calls correctly paired assertion IDs with tree person IDs across all four persons and both censuses, with recordRole properly omitted for the assertion's own party and supplied for the second party in relationship assertions (a_017, a_018). No fixture_not_found errors. research_append and materialize_facts calls correctly structured all person-evidence entries and fact enrichments.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All links are scored 'confident' with match_score 0.78, which is appropriate. The confidence is justified by: (1) exact name matches across both censuses; (2) birth years matching tree (~1822, ~1825, ~1847, ~1850); (3) multiple independent corroborating sources (1860 and 1880 censuses); (4) household position consistency (head, wife, daughter, son); (5) the LDS emigration corridor from the wiki explaining the geographic move. The move from Cranfield to Salt Lake is not a contradiction—it is explained by a documented migration corridor, so capping at 'probable' would over-fire the rule. Confidence is calibrated to the evidence strength.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites specific matching attributes: name, birth year, gender, birthplace, household position, and the LDS emigration corridor from the wiki. For example, pe_001 states 'Name Joseph Pratt exact match. Gender male matches. Birthplace England matches. Score 0.78 (strong band). All core identifiers agree; LDS emigration corridor explains England-to-Utah move.' Rationales address why competing candidates were ruled out implicitly through the strong correlation across two independent censuses with identical household composition. The move_bridge field explicitly names the corridor source.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges

No warnings on I1. All links written and checked.

---

Both records — the 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry for Hermann Gatjen and the Germans to America index entry for Herm Gaetjen arriving in New York in June 1871 — have been linked to Hermann Gaetjen in the family tree, but only at the most cautious level of certainty, **"only possibly."** Here is why, and what it means in practice.

**Why the records fit each other:**
The two records cohere well. Both give a birth year of about 1854, both point to a German immigrant heading toward California, and the timeline lines up — arriving in New York in 1871, surfacing in San Francisco by 1875, three years before his son Henry was born there. The surname spelling "Gatjen" in the voter register is a recognized Low German form of the same family name. The machine-similarity score for the voter register came back at 0.43 (the moderate range), corroborating the qualitative match. The passenger index scored very low (0.006), but that mainly reflects the truncated "Herm" first name and the nearly-empty tree record for Hermann; read alongside the voter register's 0.43 score, the low number reflects index quality, not a genuine mismatch.

**Why the links cannot be raised above "only possibly":**
The system enforces caution when other men with the same name are on file. There is a documented Hermann (Herman Conrad) Gaetjen born in San Francisco in 1873 and a Herman Gaetjen born in 1827 who died in Butte County. Both can be ruled out logically, but neither the voter register nor the passenger list mentions a family member — no wife Amelia Nichols, no children — so the system cannot automatically eliminate them. One additional complication: the voter register records naturalization on 13 August 1875, only about four years and two months after his June 1871 arrival, slightly short of the five-year residency requirement then in force; nothing on file yet explains the shortfall.

**Recommended next step:**
Find a record that names Hermann alongside Amelia Nichols or one of the children — a city directory, marriage record, census entry, or funeral notice — which would tie these voter and passenger entries firmly to your Hermann and lift the links out of the "only possibly" tier.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

No warnings on I1. All links written and checked.

---

Both records — the 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry for Hermann Gatjen and the Germans to America index entry for Herm Gaetjen arriving in New York in June 1871 — have been linked to Hermann Gaetjen in the family tree, but only at the most cautious level of certainty, "only possibly." Here is why they could not be linked more firmly, and what that means in practice.

The two records fit each other well: both give a birth year of about 1854, both point to a German immigrant who was in or heading toward California, and the timeline lines up — arriving in New York in 1871 and showing up in San Francisco by 1875, three years before his son Henry was born there. The surname spelling "Gatjen" in the voter register is a recognized Low German way of writing the same family name. The machine-similarity score for the voter register came back at 0.43 (the moderate range), which corroborates the moderate qualitative match. The passenger index scored very low (0.006), but that is almost entirely because the tree entry for Hermann has almost no facts on it — just an unverified birth year — and the index listed the first name as the truncated "Herm"; when read alongside the voter register's 0.43 score for what is very likely the same man, the low number reflects index quality and a sparse tree record, not a genuine mismatch.

The reason the links cannot be raised above "only possibly" is a protection the system enforces when other men with the same name are on file: there is a documented Hermann (Herman Conrad) Gaetjen born in San Francisco in 1873 and another Herman Gaetjen born in 1827 who died in Butte County. Both are too old or too young to be your Hermann, but the system cannot automatically rule them out without a record that names Hermann alongside someone known to be his — his wife Amelia Nichols, or one of his children — and neither the voter register nor the passenger list mentions any family member. One additional complication: the voter register says he naturalized on 13 August 1875, but his recorded arrival was 2 June 1871, giving only about four years and two months of U.S. residence rather than the five years the law at that time required; nothing on file yet explains the shortfall.

The next step is to find a record that names Hermann together with Amelia Nichols or one of the children — a city directory, a marriage record, a census, or a funeral home record — which would tie these voter and passenger entries firmly to your Hermann and lift the link out of the "only possibly" tier.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

---

## What pe_005 Covers

`a_013` is a **relationship** assertion ("Father: Thomas Flynn") from the 1908 death certificate, with informant James Brown (son-in-law, flagged `family_not_present` and `secondary`). The identity question pe_005 answers is: *Is the deceased on this certificate the same person as I1 in the tree?*

---

## Confidence Calibration: "confident" Is Defensible

The deceased is a Patrick Flynn who died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, PA — matching I1's tree death fact exactly. Two prior census records independently corroborate:

- **pe_001** (1850 census) → I1 at *confident*
- **pe_004** (1860 census) → I1 at *confident*

The named father (Thomas Flynn) aligns with I2 already in the tree and the existing ParentChild edge R1. No core identifier conflicts undermine the tier. **On substance, "confident" is justified.**

---

## Four Problems with the Written Rationale

The tier is right, but the rationale fails to show its work:

1. **Missing required format lines** — no "Date check" (tree birth year ~1845 vs. cert ~1845: gap 0 years) and no "Residence check" (Schuylkill County, 1908 vs. established 1860 residence). Both run cleanly, but are unwritten.

3. **Birth location discrepancy not addressed** — The cert's informant gave Pennsylvania as birthplace; prior censuses establish Ireland. 4. **Corroborating census links not cited** — "Death location matches known residence" is asserted without naming pe_001 or pe_004 as the basis.

`a_013` names two parties — the deceased (I1) and Thomas Flynn (I2) as father. Both-sided pe_ entries are mandatory for every relationship-implying assertion. Checking I2's entries (pe_003, pe_006), neither links a_013 to I2. **A pe_ entry linking a_013 → I2 is missing.**

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Here is the person-evidence agent's full report:

---

**Links created — both sources linked to I1 (Hermann Gaetjen), no stub needed:**

| pe_ | Assertion | Person | Confidence | Score | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| pe_008 | a_008 (voter registration: 13 Aug 1875) | I1 | probable | 0.43 | — |
| pe_009 | a_009 (sex: Male inferred) | I1 | probable | 0.43 | — |
| pe_010 | a_010 (name: Herm Gaetjen) | I1 | speculative | 0.006 | — |
| pe_011 | a_011 (sex: Male) | I1 | speculative | 0.006 | — |
| pe_012 | a_012 (birth: 1854) | I1 | speculative | 0.006 | — |
| pe_013 | a_013 (birth place: Prussia) | I1 | speculative | 0.006 | — |
| pe_014 | a_014 (immigration: 2 Jun 1871, New York) | I1 | speculative | 0.006 | Arrival only 4y 2m before naturalization — short, non-binding at speculative |

---

**Materialization:**
- Great Register (src_001) facts written onto I1: name spelling Gatjen, occupation Fireman, residence 5 Cook St SF 1875, naturalization 13 Aug 1875, voter registration, birthplace Germany, computed birth ~1854.
- Passenger index (src_002) facts **not** materialized — the speculative confidence threshold is too low to write to an existing tree person. Those facts become writable once identity is confirmed at probable or above.

---

**Birth conflict surfaced on I1:**
Two birth facts now coexist on I1 — the old unsourced "about 1859" and the newly added "~1854" from the Great Register. The system flagged this as a contradiction. **Conflict-resolution is needed** to retire the unsourced estimate and formally accept ~1854 as the working documented date.

---

**Narrative summary:**

The 1875 San Francisco Great Register records a Hermann Gatjen — almost certainly the same person who would father children in San Francisco in 1878 and 1883 — living at 5 Cook Street, working as a fireman, born in Germany, naturalized on 13 Aug 1875. This is linked to I1 at **probable** confidence (score 0.43), based on the distinctive surname, matching city, and nationality. The Germans to America passenger index then shows a Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 in Prussia, arriving in New York on 2 June 1871 — four years before the San Francisco registration. That arrival record is linked at **speculative** confidence (score 0.006) only, because the index alone offers too little to match against I1's sparse profile.

Both records agree on a birth year around 1854, conflicting with the tree's unsourced "about 1859." Since the 1859 estimate had no documentary basis, the records likely correct it. **Next step:** conflict-resolution to retire "about 1859" and accept ~1854. One open question remains: the naturalization date (August 1875) is only about four years after the New York arrival (June 1871), slightly short of the statutory five-year requirement — finding the actual naturalization court record or evidence of an earlier US residency period would resolve this.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.
